title: Git Best Practices
description: Master commit hygiene, branching discipline, and team conventions that keep Git a reliable foundation for software delivery.

data.text: Great Git habits are invisible: history stays readable, merges are rare conflicts, and new team members can navigate the repository without asking for help. These habits are not optional polish; they directly affect merge frequency, debugging speed, and onboarding time.

A commit message is documentation of intent. The first line should summarize the change in 50 characters or fewer. The body should explain why the change was made, not restate the diff. Follow a conventional format like Conventional Commits so changelogs and release notes can be automated.

data.title: Conventional commit format
data.code:
feat(auth): add OAuth2 refresh token support

Clients can now refresh expired access tokens without
prompting the user to sign in again. This reduces
session interruptions during long-lived workflows.

Fixes #1234

data.text: A commit should do one thing and do it completely. Large commits are harder to review, harder to revert, and harder to bisect. Use interactive staging to split changes into logical units before committing.

data.title: Stage part of a file
data.code:
git add -p path/to/file.cs

# For each hunk, choose:
# y - stage this hunk
# n - skip it
# s - split into smaller hunks
# q - quit

items: Delete branches after merging. Stale branches clutter the repository and confuse new team members.
Rebase feature branches on `main` before opening a pull request to keep the history linear.
Use short-lived branches. The longer a branch lives, the more likely it will conflict with `main`.

data.text: Merge commits preserve the exact chronology of parallel work. Rebases rewrite history to create a linear story. Use merge for shared branches where rewriting would disrupt collaborators. Use rebase for private feature branches before opening a pull request.

data.title: The golden rule of rebasing
data.text: Never rebase a branch that has been shared with others. Rewriting public history forces every collaborator to reconcile the divergence, which is far more disruptive than a merge commit.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Write commit messages that explain why, not what.
Keep commits small, focused, and independently reviewable.
Delete merged branches and keep feature branches short-lived.
Rebase private branches; merge shared branches.
